title: "Go, you are free"
hook: he forgives the people who drove him out, echoing Yusuf, no blame on you today (12:92)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Sufyan's city, Mecca, conquered: ten thousand at his back, and the Prophet ﷺ riding in with his head bowed so low his beard nearly touched the saddle. Your line was head bowed on the camel.

The square around the Ka'ba is full that day, and the faces are familiar. Some of these people mocked him in the street for years. Some boycotted his clan, shutting them up hungry in a narrow valley, chased him out of his hometown, and fought him at Badr and Uhud. One woman in that crowd had rejoiced over the body of his uncle Hamzah. Now the city is his, and no army is left to stop him. The early biographies say he asked them: what do you think I'm going to do to you? They answered carefully, the way you answer when your life depends on it: good. You're a noble brother, the son of a noble brother.
screen: `THE PEOPLE WHO DROVE HIM OUT.` → `WHAT DO YOU THINK I'LL DO?` → `GOOD, NOBLE BROTHER.`

segments.voice: According to the early accounts of his life, he said: I say to you what Yusuf said to his brothers. No blame on you today. Go, you are free. He didn't make up a speech. He reached for a story everyone listening knew. In the Qur'an's twelfth surah, Joseph's brothers throw him into a well, and he is sold away. Years later they stand before him in Egypt, hungry, not knowing who he is, and when they finally realize, they're ashamed. And Yusuf says, in the Qur'an's words, that there is no blame on them this day, and that God will forgive them. The Prophet stepped into that story on purpose: you're my brothers, and I'm doing what Yusuf did. The reports call the people of Mecca after this the tulaqa', the freed ones. Notice what this forgiveness is not. It isn't pretending nothing happened; everyone in that square knew exactly what had happened, and that's why they were afraid. It isn't weakness either; he could have done anything. It's choosing, from strength, not to collect the debt. Some of the people let go that day became Muslims, and some later became leaders of the community. Muslim teachers often point out that some were his own relatives. Family is often the hardest place to say: go, you're free.
screen: `WHAT YUSUF SAID TO HIS BROTHERS.` · `NO BLAME ON YOU TODAY.` · `TULAQA' — THE FREED ONES.` · `FORGIVING FROM STRENGTH.` · then, large: `GO, YOU ARE FREE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who hurt you long ago: not the worst thing that ever happened to you, just something you've carried a while. You don't have to call them or say it was fine; just picture them and see if you can let the debt go, even a little. If you pray, you can ask God to forgive them, and you; if you don't, just try the words quietly: go, you're free.
Go. The first word of what he told the people who'd driven him out: go, you are free. Today's word.
Your line: no blame on you today. Yusuf said it first. Day two hundred seventy-eight, done.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the forgiveness at the conquest of Mecca as a model of mercy, and many teachers use it, together with Yusuf's words to his brothers, when urging people to forgive relatives and old enemies.

original.note: Arabic: the freed ones, the name given to the people of Mecca let go that day.

what a scholar hears: he frames it as Yusuf's words to his brothers (12:92), turning the conquest into a family reunion; the people of Mecca became the tulaqa'.

chat.says: What did the Prophet say to the people of Mecca who had driven him out?
options: Yusuf's words to his brothers: no blame on you today. Go, you are free.
That they could stay, but only if they all became Muslim that day.
That he forgave them, but they had to leave Mecca for good.
chat.meaning: He reached for Yusuf's words: no blame on you today. He chose, from strength, not to collect the debt.

Yusuf.meaning: the prophet Joseph, who forgave the brothers who wronged him

tulaqa'.meaning: the freed ones: the people of Mecca let go that day

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: removed 'some had thrown filth on him while he prayed' (Bukhari 240 says the men behind that were killed at Badr, so they were not in the crowd) and the unsourced 'three years'; hook no longer opens 'Picture'; the teach wrongly called tulaqa' 'our word today' (the word is 'Go'), cut; Yusuf's brothers 'ashamed' (12:91), not 'terrified'; 'many became Muslims' softened in teach and myth.

The 'go, you are free' (idhhabu fa-antum at-tulaqa') report is from Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham and later collections (e.g. al-Bayhaqi); hadith scholars have questioned its chain. The script says 'according to the early accounts'. Confirm this framing.
The woman who rejoiced over Hamzah's body (Hind bint Utbah) is alluded to without naming her; she accepted Islam at the conquest. Confirm the allusion is appropriate.
'Some had thrown filth on him while he prayed' refers to the camel-entrails incident (Sahih al-Bukhari 240); confirm.
The word for this day is the index's title head, '"Go'; the word screen shows the whole phrase. The owner may want a cleaner index word (e.g. tulaqa').
12:92 paraphrased rather than quoted from Pickthall; a Keeper may wish to add the Pickthall wording.
